record.narrative: Registering a first set of 12 falsifiable binary-marker comparisons in the supplied lung cancer CRISPR screen dataset. Because dependency scores are more negative when dependency is stronger, direction -1 means the exposed group is expected to have lower/stronger dependency, while direction +1 means the exposed group is expected to have higher/weaker dependency. The first comparisons target well-motivated biomarker-dependency relationships: KRAS mutation should strengthen KRAS dependency; BRAF V600E should strengthen BRAF dependency; EGFR and ERBB2 amplifications should strengthen EGFR/ERBB2 dependency if amplifications are driver-like; TP53 loss should weaken MDM2 dependency because MDM2 is most relevant to p53-WT contexts; MSI-high should strengthen WRN dependency; SMARCA4 loss should create SMARCA2 dependency through SWI/SNF paralog/complementation logic; KEAP1 loss should strengthen NFE2L2/NRF2 dependency through pathway activation; KRAS-mutant lines may depend less on RIT1 because KRAS itself is the dominant Ras-family driver; MYC amplification is used as a marker of transcriptional/translational/proliferative stress and may strengthen dependency on USP7, KIF18A, and RPL11. I registered all claims as unresolved because no direct evidence exists yet. I will later judge scientific meaningfulness using both the 10% clinical-significance notion and the scale/variance of the dependency score, with emphasis on whether 95% intervals exclude trivial differences. Planned follow-ups include dependency_DHX9, dependency_POLR2A, dependency_STAT3, dependency_TMED10, additional SMARCA2/ARID1A relationships, subgroups by lineage_subtype or co-mutation status, and technical predictors such as CRISPR library or screen QC if biological hypotheses appear to be confounded by assay variation.

Requesting discovery analyses for the first 12 registered comparisons because they cover the most biologically motivated driver-biomarker associations and all have enough observations in the exposed and comparator groups to satisfy the 20-observation cell rule. I am prioritizing direct driver-gene dependencies (KRAS, BRAF, EGFR, ERBB2), well-established pathway-loss dependencies (MDM2/TP53, WRN/MSI, SMARCA2/SMARCA4, NFE2L2/KEAP1), a pathway-specific Ras-family hypothesis (RIT1 in KRAS-mutant lines), and MYC amplification as a broad marker for transcriptional/translational/cell-cycle stress dependencies (USP7, KIF18A, RPL11). These results will establish which hypotheses have signal and guide follow-up subgroup or technical-control analyses.

The first discovery set gives three robust findings and many mostly null driver associations. H6 is accepted: MSI-high lines have much stronger WRN dependency than MSI-low lines. The signed estimate +0.789 for direction -1 means the raw exposed-minus-comparator difference is about -0.789, i.e. MSI-high cells are far more negative/dependent; the 95% interval entirely excludes zero and is huge relative to WRN's score distribution. H7 is accepted: SMARCA4-loss lines show much stronger SMARCA2 dependency than SMARCA4-intact lines, again a very large raw negative shift with a tight interval excluding zero. H8 is rejected in the registered direction because the interval strongly indicates the opposite relationship: KEAP1-loss lines have weaker NFE2L2 dependency, not stronger dependency. This is scientifically plausible because KEAP1 loss activates NRF2/NFE2L2 pathway signaling, potentially reducing the incremental effect of knocking out NFE2L2 itself, but the registered claim was the opposite direction, so the claim itself must be rejected and a reversed comparison registered. H3 EGFR amplification versus EGFR dependency is the most useful validation target: the signed estimate +0.0252 is about a 10% shift relative to the average absolute EGFR dependency score, but the interval is borderline near zero, so I leave it unresolved and request independent validation. H1 KRAS is borderline and unresolved: the signed point estimate is positive and supports the hypothesized stronger KRAS dependency, but the interval includes zero and only partly includes clinically meaningful magnitude, so it is too weak to accept. I keep it active for subgroup refinement. H2, H9, and H12 are rejected for the registered direction because their intervals do not support a meaningful effect in the anticipated direction; in H2 and H12 the upper bound for hypothesis-supporting magnitude is below about 10% of the score distribution, and in H9 the maximum hypothesis-supporting effect is also below the approximate 10% threshold. H4, H5, H10, and H11 remain unresolved but not promising: their intervals include either null or clinically meaningful effects in both directions or only weak support, so I do not accept them and close them to current follow-up unless a stronger marker or interaction emerges. Overall, the evidence best supports WRN/MSI, SMARCA2/SMARCA4-loss, and KEAP1-loss/NFE2L2 inverse association, while classical RTK driver-biomarker associations in this dataset are weak or borderline.

The requested independent validation resolves H3 against the EGFR-amplification dependency hypothesis. The discovery evidence R3 pointed weakly toward stronger EGFR dependency in EGFR-amplified lines (signed estimate +0.025 relative to the registered negative direction), but its interval crossed zero and only barely included a roughly 10% clinically meaningful shift. The validation evidence R13, reported with a much more conservative independent interval, had the opposite signed point estimate (-0.022), with an interval from about -0.064 to +0.019. Its upper bound for the registered hypothesis direction is below the approximate 0.025 clinical-magnitude threshold, while the point estimate and interval are compatible with no effect or the opposite direction. Thus the original global claim that EGFR amplification is associated with stronger EGFR dependency is not supported and is rejected. This does not establish causality or generalizability; it only means this dataset does not support the registered association. I still keep an interaction refinement to ask whether a small adenocarcinoma-restricted effect exists, but the main EGFR-amplification claim should not be accepted.

The strongest current dataset-supported findings are: MSI-high cells have much stronger WRN dependency; SMARCA4-loss cells have much stronger SMARCA2 dependency; and KEAP1-loss cells have much weaker NFE2L2 dependency. H13 should now be accepted. Its evidence R8, when signed to the reversed +1 direction, gives a very large positive contrast (about +0.80) with a very tight interval excluding zero. Biologically, KEAP1 loss activates NRF2/NFE2L2 pathway output, which could plausibly reduce the incremental fitness effect of NFE2L2 knockout, yielding weaker NFE2L2 dependency scores in KEAP1-loss cells. This remains an association in this supplied dataset, not proof of mechanism or external generalizability.

For next analyses, I will prioritize ARID1A-loss versus SMARCA2 dependency because SWI/SNF paralog relationships are mechanistically parallel to the SMARCA4-loss finding. I will also test whether KRAS and EGFR effects are restricted to adenocarcinoma using both subgroup estimates and interactions. To avoid over-interpreting null driver-biomarker associations, I add a technical library-control comparison using Avana library exposure and dependency_POLR2A; if library exposure shifts POLR2A by a meaningful amount, that will help interpret whether technical variation contributes to null biological associations.

The current dataset-supported associations are unusually large for WRN/MSI-high, SMARCA2/SMARCA4 loss, and weaker NFE2L2 dependency in KEAP1 loss. The next explore stage focuses on whether these are context-robust associations or reflections of co-mutation, subtype, proliferation state, or screen artifacts. I add refinements that isolate SMARCA4 loss among ARID1A-intact cells and ARID1A loss among SMARCA4-intact cells to test whether SMARCA2 dependency is specific to SMARCA4 loss or reflects broader SWI/SNF lesions. Similarly, I test KEAP1 loss among STK11-intact cells and STK11 loss among KEAP1-intact cells because KEAP1 and STK11 often co-occur in lung adenocarcinoma models; this distinguishes a KEAP1/NRF2 association from a co-mutational marker effect. For WRN, I test whether the MSI-high effect remains in adenocarcinoma and across fast-growing and slower-growing cultures, since replication-stress dependencies can be proliferation-dependent. I also refine the null MYC-amplification/RPL11 claim by restricting to cells with high MYC expression, a marker-quality test for whether the binary amplification call is biologically informative when transcriptional MYC output is also high. Finally, I add technical and negative-control probes: an Avana-library association for WRN and an association with a research marker that has no assigned biological role. These help detect whether broad screen variation or arbitrary assay associations could affect interpretation. These remain associations within this supplied dataset, not causal claims or externally generalizable conclusions.

I am requesting the 12 analyses that best test whether the three strongest existing dataset associations are specific and robust rather than artifacts of co-mutation, subtype, growth state, random assay noise, or screen-library variation. For SMARCA2, H28 tests SMARCA4 loss while requiring ARID1A to be intact, H29 tests ARID1A loss while requiring SMARCA4 to be intact, H30 tests SMARCA4 loss within adenocarcinoma, and H31 tests SMARCA4 loss in faster-growing cultures. These distinguish paralog-specific SWI/SNF biology from a broad complex-deficient marker or context effect. For NFE2L2, H32 tests KEAP1 loss among STK11-intact lines and H33 tests STK11 loss among KEAP1-intact lines, which is important because KEAP1 and STK11 frequently co-occur in lung models and the accepted NFE2L2 association could be confounded by co-mutational state. For WRN, H34-H36 test the MSI-high association in adenocarcinoma, faster-growing lines, and slower-growing lines, checking whether the replication-stress dependency is subtype- and proliferation-robust. I also include H15 to follow up the borderline KRAS-mutation association in adenocarcinoma, where driver effects are most expected. Finally, H38 and H39 provide control analyses: H38 tests Avana-library exposure against the accepted WRN outcome, and H39 tests a research marker with no assigned biological role against the accepted SMARCA2 outcome. These controls help determine whether accepted large effects could be partly technical or whether an unexplained dataset structure could produce large marker-association contrasts.

The new discovery set strongly reinforces the three largest accepted dataset associations and makes them more specific. H28/R14 shows that SMARCA4 loss is still associated with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency when restricted to ARID1A-intact cells; the signed estimate is about +0.777 for the negative dependency-direction claim, meaning the raw exposed-minus-comparator difference is roughly -0.777. This is enormous relative to SMARCA2 score scale, so H28 is accepted. H29/R15 tests ARID1A loss among SMARCA4-intact cells and gives a tiny, direction-inconsistent contrast (signed -0.003), with a maximum hypothesis-supporting magnitude well below the approximate 10% SMARCA2 scale; H29 is rejected. Thus the SMARCA2 association looks much more specific to SMARCA4 loss than to ARID1A loss in this selected dataset.

H30 and H31 accept SMARCA4 loss within adenocarcinoma and faster-growing lines, respectively. These subgroup effects are nearly as large as the global effect, although H31 is restricted to measured growth-rate cases. H32/R18 accepts the co-mutation-isolated reversed NFE2L2 finding: among STK11-intact lines, KEAP1 loss is associated with weaker NFE2L2 dependency (signed +0.801 for the positive direction, i.e. less negative dependency). This is very large and supports specificity to KEAP1 rather than STK11. H33/R19 tests STK11 loss among KEAP1-intact lines and is essentially null; because the NFE2L2 score distribution and registered direction make the exact 10% boundary somewhat sensitive, I leave H33 unresolved but closed as not promising. I request independent validation of H32 because it is a refined, biologically important reversal claim and is well powered.

H34, H35, and H36 accept MSI-high versus WRN dependency in adenocarcinoma, faster-growing lines, and slower-growing lines, respectively. The lower bounds remain far above clinical-magnitude thresholds, even though H36 has a smaller exposed cell (25) and wider interval. The MSI-high WRN association appears robust across available subtype and growth-rate contexts. H15/R23 remains unresolved: KRAS-mutant adenocarcinoma lines show a weak positive signed contrast consistent with stronger KRAS dependency, but the interval includes both null and clinically meaningful effects; this is not enough to accept.

The control probes are reassuring but not absolutely perfect. H38/R24 tests Avana-library exposure for WRN in the registered positive direction; the signed estimate is negative and the upper bound for a positive library effect is below the approximate 10% WRN threshold, so the registered positive association is rejected. A modest inverse library association is not excluded, but it is small relative to the accepted MSI-high effect. H39/R25 tests an arbitrary research marker against SMARCA2; no clinically meaningful positive contrast is present, supporting that the SMARCA2 finding is not driven by an unassigned binary assay. Overall, the evidence now supports co-mutation-isolated and context-robust dataset associations for SMARCA4-loss/SMARCA2 and MSI-high/WRN, with strong dataset support for KEAP1-loss/weaker NFE2L2 that is pending independent validation.

The independent validation of H32 is decisive and strengthens the accepted KEAP1-loss association for weaker NFE2L2 dependency. H32 asks whether, among STK11-intact lines, KEAP1 loss is associated with weaker NFE2L2 dependency, i.e. a positive exposed-minus-comparator contrast because less negative dependency means weaker dependency. The discovery evidence R18 gave a signed estimate of +0.801 with a 95% interval from about +0.779 to +0.823. The new independent validation R26 is even stronger: signed estimate +0.815, with a very conservative independent interval from +0.782 to +0.847. Both estimates are far above the approximate clinically meaningful magnitude threshold for this outcome distribution and exclude zero decisively. Therefore H32 is accepted and its investigation can be closed. The result remains an association in this supplied dataset and should not be interpreted as proof of causality or external generalizability, but it is among the most robust dataset-supported findings here.

The overall supported evidence now centers on three biological associations. First, MSI-high lines have much stronger WRN dependency. The global H6 estimate is about +0.790 signed toward stronger dependency, with interval +0.760 to +0.819. This is robust in adenocarcinoma, faster-growing lines, and slower-growing lines, with H34, H35, and H36 all giving very large lower bounds. Second, SMARCA4 loss is associated with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency. The global H7 estimate is about +0.784 signed toward stronger dependency, interval +0.765 to +0.803, and it remains large when restricted to ARID1A-intact lines, adenocarcinoma, and faster-growing lines. ARID1A loss in SMARCA4-intact lines is essentially null, so the SMARCA2 finding is more specific to SMARCA4 loss than to SWI/SNF lesions generally in this dataset. Third, KEAP1 loss is associated with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency. The reversed H13 claim is supported globally, and the validated co-mutation-isolated H32 claim is now strongly supported. STK11 loss among KEAP1-intact lines is not meaningfully associated with weaker NFE2L2 dependency, helping distinguish KEAP1 from STK11 co-mutational confounding.

Negative findings are also informative. The global EGFR-amplification claim H3 was rejected after discovery plus independent validation; the validated interval favored no effect or the opposite direction. BRAF V600E to stronger BRAF dependency H2, KRAS mutation to RIT1 dependency H9, and MYC amplification to stronger RPL11 dependency H12 were also rejected for the registered direction. Control comparisons suggest that the large accepted effects are not explained by the tested arbitrary assay or the tested positive Avana-library direction: marker E was not associated with SMARCA2 in a clinically meaningful way, and Avana exposure was not associated with stronger WRN dependency, though a modest inverse library association remains possible. 

Important uncertainty remains. KRAS-mutation association with KRAS dependency is weak globally and in adenocarcinoma; the intervals include both null and clinically meaningful effects, so it remains unresolved. Many broader pathway and marker hypotheses remain untested or only partially tested, including EGFR adenocarcinoma-specific and interaction claims, STAT3 and TMED10 associations with RTK amplifications, MYC-related DHX9 and POLR2A claims, ARID1A broad claim H14, WRN BRCA2 claim, RIT1 NF1 claim, the POLR2A library control, and high-MYC-expression RPL11 refinement. The next most informative analyses should combine these pending broad comparisons with newly registered robustness tests for the accepted effects: higher screen-quality restriction and Avana-library subsets for WRN/SMARCA2/NFE2L2 associations, plus co-loss probes for KEAP1 with STK11 and SMARCA4 with ARID1A. These will clarify whether the large accepted effects persist under technical-quality restriction and how much they depend on co-occurring genomic alterations.

The registered new comparisons keep the focus on both robustness of the strongest dataset-supported associations and expansion into untested predictors. For WRN/MSI-high, SMARCA2/SMARCA4 loss, and KEAP1 loss/weaker NFE2L2 dependency, I add reliability and context restrictions: matched RNA/DNA availability and low-serum culture conditions. These probe whether the very large associations persist when genomic calls may be better supported and under a simpler culture condition. For accepted associations, I explicitly attach parent claims and available motivating evidence only where a parent has evidence. The broader set asks whether RB1 loss is associated with stronger WRN dependency, whether PIK3CA mutation has any association with STAT3 dependency, whether the weak EGFR/ERBB2 driver signals become informative in adenocarcinoma or after removing TP53 co-loss, and whether NF1 loss is associated with stronger RIT1 dependency after excluding KRAS-mutant lines. A marker-D negative control against WRN tests whether an unassigned binary assay produces a clinically meaningful positive contrast, helping assess whether large WRN associations are not merely driven by arbitrary assay variation. All hypotheses remain associations within this supplied dataset, not causal or generalizable conclusions.

I am selecting 12 analyses that combine focused robustness/co-loss tests for the strongest accepted dataset associations with several high-value unresolved and negative-control probes. For WRN/MSI-high, H50 tests whether the large association persists when only matched RNA/DNA profiles are used, and H43 tests whether it remains under stricter screen-quality restriction using screen_roc_auc >= 0.95. These address whether the accepted WRN effect is stable under better genomic-call reliability and high-quality CRISPR screens. For SMARCA2, H52 tests the SMARCA4-loss effect under matched RNA/DNA availability, while H49 tests the complementary co-loss situation: SMARCA4 loss among ARID1A-loss lines. H49 is important because H28 showed the effect is strong when ARID1A is intact; H49 tests whether the association persists when the two SWI/SNF lesions co-occur. For NFE2L2, H48 tests KEAP1 loss among STK11-loss lines, complementing the already validated H32 test among STK11-intact lines and helping determine whether the KEAP1 association is robust to STK11 co-loss rather than only an isolated co-mutational marker effect. The broad set then targets remaining unresolved driver and pathway questions: H16 asks whether EGFR amplification has an adenocarcinoma-specific association after the global EGFR claim was rejected; H59 asks whether KRAS-mutation dependency becomes clearer among TP53-intact lines, isolating the driver from a common co-loss; H60 asks whether NF1 loss is associated with stronger RIT1 dependency after excluding KRAS-mutant lines; H56 tests RB1 loss as another replication/cell-cycle-related predictor of WRN dependency; H57 tests PIK3CA mutation as a STAT3-pathway predictor; and H37 refines the MYC/RPL11 null by using high transcriptomic MYC rather than binary amplification. Finally, H61 is a negative control using research marker D against WRN, the same outcome as the accepted MSI-high effect, to assess whether an unassigned binary assay can produce a large positive contrast. This mix should either strengthen specificity of the accepted associations or reveal additional scientifically meaningful dataset associations, while keeping all conclusions limited to this supplied dataset.

The new robustness and co-mutation analyses further strengthen the three largest dataset-supported associations while providing useful negative controls. For WRN/MSI-high, H43/R27 shows that the association remains extremely large under stricter screen-quality restriction, with signed estimate about +0.795 and lower bound +0.758, far above the approximate 10% WRN clinical-magnitude threshold around +0.03. H50/R30 shows the same near-global effect under matched RNA/DNA availability, with lower bound about +0.760. These results support accepting H43 and H50 and closing them as accepted context-robust refinements. For SMARCA2/SMARCA4 loss, H52/R31 shows the effect remains huge under matched RNA/DNA availability, lower bound about +0.760, far above the approximate SMARCA2 threshold around +0.04. H49/R29 is especially informative because it tests SMARCA4 loss specifically among ARID1A-loss lines: the signed effect is about +0.814 with lower bound +0.767, indicating the association is not weakened when SWI/SNF co-loss is present. This is a strong new accepted refinement, but because the exposed cell is small (n=76) and this is a newly accepted claim, I request independent validation of H49. For NFE2L2/KEAP1 loss, H48/R28 tests KEAP1 loss among STK11-loss lines and gives a very large positive signed effect, lower bound +0.727, far above the small NFE2L2 absolute-scale clinical threshold around +0.009. This complements the already validated STK11-intact H32 result and supports that the KEAP1 association is not limited to one co-mutational stratum.

The negative and borderline claims are mostly unhelpful. H57/R33 tests PIK3CA mutation for stronger STAT3 dependency; the signed estimate is opposite the registered direction and the upper bound for hypothesis-supporting effect is well below the approximate STAT3 threshold, so H57 is rejected. H60/R35 tests NF1 loss among KRAS-wildtype lines for stronger RIT1 dependency; the registered positive-support interval does not reach the RIT1 clinical threshold, so H60 is rejected. H61/R36 is a useful negative control using research marker D against WRN; the upper positive bound is far below the WRN threshold, supporting that arbitrary binary assay structure does not reproduce the large MSI-high effect. H56/R32 remains unresolved but closed: RB1 loss shows a small positive point estimate for WRN dependency, but the interval includes null and some clinically meaningful values, while the point estimate is not compelling. H59/R34 also remains unresolved but closed: KRAS-mutant TP53-intact lines show a small positive signed effect for KRAS dependency, but the interval includes null and values above threshold; this is not enough to accept. H16/R37 is a borderline EGFR-amplification subgroup test: it remains unresolved but closed because the point estimate is below threshold and the global EGFR claim was already independently rejected; H37/R38 similarly remains unresolved but closed because the estimate is essentially null despite an interval that barely includes clinically meaningful positive effects. Overall, the evidence continues to support WRN dependence in MSI-high lines, SMARCA2 dependence in SMARCA4-loss lines, and weaker NFE2L2 dependence in KEAP1-loss lines, with these findings remaining dataset-specific associations rather than causal or generalizable claims.

The newly released validation for H28 and H49 decisively confirms the SMARCA2/SMARCA4-loss association as the second major dataset-supported finding after WRN/MSI-high, while the H3 validation response resolves the EGFR-amplification claim against the registered stronger-dependency hypothesis.

First, H3 asked whether EGFR amplification is associated with stronger EGFR dependency, direction -1. Discovery R3 gave a signed estimate of about +0.025 with interval from about -0.000 to +0.051. This was near the approximate 10%-of-absolute-mean EGFR score threshold around +0.025, but the interval included null and could not support acceptance. The independent validation R13 is now available and is signed opposite the registered stronger-dependency direction: estimate about -0.022, interval about -0.064 to +0.019. The upper bound of the hypothesis-supporting interval is below the approximate clinical-magnitude threshold of +0.025 and the point estimate favors the opposite direction, i.e. weaker EGFR dependency with EGFR amplification. H3 is therefore rejected and closed. I registered a reversal proposal for weaker EGFR dependency with EGFR amplification because the validated data suggest that possibility, but the reversal interval still includes null and the discovery point estimate favored the opposite direction, so it remains unresolved and should not be accepted.

Second, H28 tested SMARCA4 loss among ARID1A-intact lines for stronger SMARCA2 dependency. Discovery R14 gave signed estimate +0.777 with lower bound +0.756; independent validation R40 gives estimate +0.812 with lower bound +0.778. These are vastly larger than the approximate SMARCA2 meaningful threshold around +0.042. H28 is accepted and closed. This shows that the strong SMARCA4-loss effect is not explained by ARID1A-intact selection alone; it remains enormous even when ARID1A loss is excluded.

Third, H49 tested the complementary co-loss situation: SMARCA4 loss among ARID1A-loss lines for stronger SMARCA2 dependency. Discovery R29 gave signed estimate +0.814 with lower bound +0.767; independent validation R39 gives estimate +0.811 with lower bound +0.743. This again far exceeds the approximate SMARCA2 clinical threshold. H49 is accepted and closed. Together with H7, H28, H30, H31, and H52, the evidence supports that SMARCA2 dependency is strongly and specifically associated with SMARCA4 loss, regardless of ARID1A status. The ARID1A-only effect among SMARCA4-intact lines (H29/R15) remains null, reinforcing that ARID1A loss alone is not the driver.

The broader evidence now supports three main dataset-specific associations:
1. MSI-high status is associated with much stronger WRN dependency. The global H6 estimate is signed +0.790 with lower bound +0.760; this is far above the approximate WRN threshold around +0.030. It remains robust in adenocarcinoma, faster and slower growth strata, higher screen-quality restriction, and matched RNA/DNA subsets.
2. SMARCA4 loss is associated with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency. Global H7 is signed +0.784, lower bound +0.765, and validations/subgroup restrictions remain far above threshold.
3. KEAP1 loss is associated with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency. The reversed global claim H13/R8 is signed +0.796, and the validated STK11-intact H32/R18/R26 is signed about +0.80 to +0.81. H48/R28 shows the same large weaker-dependency association among STK11-loss lines, with lower bound +0.727. This effect is therefore co-mutation robust in this dataset.

Negative findings are also useful. EGFR amplification is not supported for stronger EGFR dependency after validation. BRAF V600E for stronger BRAF dependency, KRAS mutation for stronger RIT1 dependency, MYC amplification for stronger RPL11 dependency, PIK3CA mutation for stronger STAT3 dependency, and NF1 loss among KRAS-wildtype lines for stronger RIT1 dependency are rejected for the registered directions. ARID1A loss among SMARCA4-intact lines is essentially null. Control tests with research markers and Avana-library positive-direction hypotheses have not produced clinically meaningful effects comparable to the accepted associations, although library and assay negative controls are not exhaustive.

Important uncertainty remains. KRAS mutation effects on KRAS dependency are weak globally and in adenocarcinoma; I have marked H1/H15 deferred as low-priority unresolved claims unless future interaction or quality-restricted tests change that assessment. The possible opposite EGFR-amplification/weaker EGFR dependency association remains unresolved and was formally registered. Broad untested associations still include ARID1A global SMARCA2, STAT3/TMED10 with RTK amplifications, MYC-related DHX9/POLR2A/USP7/KIF18A effects, WRN/BRCA2, RIT1/NF1 global, lineage interactions, and library/low-serum robustness tests.

The most informative next analysis should prioritize: formal interaction and within-stratum co-loss tests for the accepted associations, especially SMARCA4 x ARID1A and KEAP1 x STK11 specificity; the EGFR reversal claim; remaining broad untested pathway associations; and matched-direction research-marker controls. All conclusions remain associations in this supplied lung-cell-line dataset, not causal effects or generalizable claims.

The next comparisons are designed to test whether the large accepted dataset associations are robust to technical and biological context, and whether less-resolved driver/pathway claims become clearer after co-alteration or transcriptomic filtering. For the three accepted effects, I registered stricter context tests: high mutation burden for WRN/MSI-high to probe whether the association is merely a generic high-mutation-burden artifact; Ky-library subsets to test whether the associations survive an alternative CRISPR screening platform rather than being specific to the dominant Avana library; and very high screen ROC for SMARCA2/SMARCA4 loss and NFE2L2/KEAP1 loss, paralleling the already accepted high-quality-screen restriction for WRN. Persistence under these conditions would strengthen confidence that these are not technical artifacts, while attenuation would suggest quality- or library-dependent associations. For pathway isolation, I registered EGFR-amplification-negative ERBB2 and ERBB2-amplification-negative EGFR comparisons, with the EGFR claim in the weaker-dependency direction suggested by prior validation, to assess whether RTK amplification effects are diluted by co-amplification. I also registered KRAS-mutation dependency under high screen quality, TP53-loss MDM2 dependency among CDKN2A-intact lines, and BRAF-mutant RIT1 dependency among KRAS-wildtype lines. Finally, because binary MYC amplification was globally near-null for several MYC-related dependencies, I registered MYC-amplification tests restricted to high transcriptomic MYC expression, where amplification is more likely to be transcriptionally active. All claims remain associations in this supplied dataset, not causal or generalizable effects.

I selected 12 analyses that together stress-test the three strongest accepted dataset associations and add high-value specificity or pathway-isolation tests. H69 tests whether the WRN/MSI-high association persists among relatively high mutation-burden lines, reducing the concern that MSI-high is only a generic high-TMB marker. H70 tests WRN/MSI-high specifically in the alternative KY library, asking whether the huge accepted effect is restricted to the dominant Avana screen. H71 and H73 apply very high screen-quality restriction to SMARCA4-loss/SMARCA2 and KEAP1-loss/NFE2L2, respectively; H72 and H74 test those accepted effects in KY. Together, these six newly registered robustness claims probe technical platform, screen quality, and mutation-burden context. H64 and H66 are registered interactions that assess whether the magnitude of SMARCA4-loss SMARCA2 dependency differs by ARID1A loss and whether KEAP1-loss weaker NFE2L2 dependency differs by STK11 loss, beyond the already accepted within-stratum restrictions. H75 and H76 isolate RTK amplification signals by excluding co-amplification: H75 tests ERBB2-amplification stronger ERBB2 dependency among EGFR-amplification-negative lines, while H76 tests the unresolved opposite EGFR-amplification weaker EGFR dependency direction among ERBB2-amplification-negative lines. H79 tests BRAF V600E-associated stronger RIT1 dependency among KRAS-wildtype lines as an RAS/MAPK-pathway alternative to the rejected KRAS and NF1 analyses. H82 tests MYC-amplification stronger USP7 dependency only among transcriptionally high-MYC lines, where amplification is more likely to be biologically active than in the global near-null MYC-amplification claims. These selections prioritize new evidence rather than rerunning already tested comparisons.

The new robustness analyses strongly support the three major dataset-specific associations and do not materially change their interpretation. Approximate 10% relative thresholds based on population absolute means are about +0.030 for WRN, +0.042 for SMARCA2, +0.009 for NFE2L2, +0.025 for EGFR, +0.026 for ERBB2, +0.026 for RIT1, and +0.018 for USP7. For WRN/MSI-high, H69/R41 in high-mutation-burden lines gives a signed effect +0.782 with lower bound +0.749, and H70/R42 in the alternative KY library gives +0.732 with lower bound +0.675. Both intervals are far above the WRN clinical-magnitude threshold and far from null. H69 therefore addresses the concern that MSI-high is merely a generic high-TMB marker: the WRN association persists among lines selected for relatively high mutation burden. H70 addresses platform specificity: the association is still enormous in KY, despite the exposed cell having only 32 lines. These accept H69 and H70 as robust dataset-specific refinements, though I note the small exposed cell in H70 and rely on the consistency with the global effect and many prior strata. For SMARCA2/SMARCA4 loss, H71/R43 under very high screen-quality restriction and H72/R44 in KY both yield huge positive signed effects (+0.793 and +0.816) with lower bounds above +0.75. These are well above the approximate SMARCA2 threshold and support accepting both as robust dataset-specific refinements. For NFE2L2/KEAP1 loss, H73/R45 under very high screen-quality restriction and H74/R46 in KY both yield very large weaker-dependency effects (+0.797 and +0.794) with lower bounds above +0.75. These are far above the small NFE2L2 absolute-mean threshold and support accepting both. Together, H69-H74 strengthen the core triad against mutation-burden, screen-quality, and library-platform concerns. The interaction results are much less informative. H64/R47 asks whether the SMARCA4-loss effect on SMARCA2 differs by ARID1A loss; the interaction is +0.037 with interval -0.015 to +0.089. This is near the SMARCA2 threshold but includes null and cannot establish meaningful effect modification. Given the already accepted within-stratum effects in ARID1A-intact and ARID1A-loss groups, I leave it unresolved and closed. H66/R48 asks whether the KEAP1-loss effect on NFE2L2 differs by STK11 loss; the interaction is -0.026 with interval -0.079 to +0.026. It includes null and supports neither a clinically meaningful enhancement nor attenuation in the registered direction, so it remains unresolved and closed. RTK isolation tests are mostly null. H75/R49 tests stronger ERBB2 dependency among EGFR-amplification-negative lines and gives a near-zero estimate +0.001 with interval -0.028 to +0.030. Because the interval includes null and clinically meaningful positive values, H75 is unresolved but closed. H76/R50 tests weaker EGFR dependency among ERBB2-amplification-negative lines and gives signed estimate -0.027 with interval -0.053 to -0.001. For the registered weaker-dependency direction, this interval is entirely opposite the hypothesis, so H76 is rejected. It does suggest the opposite possibility that EGFR amplification may be associated with stronger EGFR dependency when ERBB2 amplification is absent, but the opposite-direction interval after sign reversal would only barely clear null and not robustly clear threshold, so I registered a new unresolved refinement rather than accepting it. H79/R51 tests BRAF V600E stronger RIT1 dependency among KRAS-wildtype lines; the signed point estimate is negative and the upper bound +0.021 is below the approximate RIT1 threshold +0.026. The interval does not support a clinically meaningful RIT1-dependency increase, so H79 is rejected and closed. H82/R52 tests MYC amplification stronger USP7 dependency among high MYC-expression lines. The signed point estimate +0.029 is above the approximate USP7 threshold +0.018, but the interval -0.037 to +0.095 is wide, includes null, and includes clinically meaningful opposite values. There is not enough evidence to accept or reject clinically meaningful USP7 association, so H82 remains unresolved and closed. I request independent validation of H6, the original global WRN/MSI-high association, because WRN is the largest accepted dataset-specific association and, unlike SMARCA2 and NFE2L2, it has not yet received independent validation. If validation remains large and positive, it will substantially strengthen confidence that the WRN/MSI-high finding is not a discovery-set artifact. All conclusions remain associations in this supplied dataset, not causal claims or generalizable biology.

The newly delivered validation resolves the requested original WRN claim and satisfies the response deadline for the KEAP1/STK11-intact NFE2L2 claim. For H6, MSI-high versus MSI-low/non-MSI status is associated with a far stronger WRN CRISPR dependency. Independent validation R53 gives a signed estimate of +0.7896 with an independent interval from +0.7364 to +0.8429 in cells of 117 versus 1883 lines. The approximate 10% relative clinical threshold for WRN, using the population absolute mean score of about 0.301, is about +0.030. The validation point estimate and lower bound are roughly 25 to 30 times that threshold and are nearly identical to the discovery estimate +0.7899 (R6). Therefore the WRN/MSI-high finding is not a discovery-set or small-stratum artifact; H6 is accepted and closed. This strengthens the broader WRN evidence, which already includes high mutation burden (H69/R41), KY library (H70/R42), high screen quality (H43/R27), matched RNA/DNA availability (H50/R30), and growth/lineage restrictions (H34-H36). All remain dataset-specific associations, not causal or generalizable claims.

For H32, KEAP1 loss among STK11-intact lines is associated with weaker NFE2L2 dependency. Independent validation R26 gives estimate +0.8147, interval +0.7822 to +0.8473, with cells of 309 versus 1325. The approximate 10% threshold for NFE2L2, using the population absolute mean score of about 0.093, is about +0.0093. The validation lower bound is about 84 times that threshold. This confirms the discovery estimate +0.8012 (R18) and, together with H13/R8, H48/R28, H73/R45, and H74/R46, supports that the KEAP1-loss/weaker-NFE2L2 association is large and context robust in this dataset. H32 remains accepted and closed.

The current supported dataset-specific core findings are: (1) MSI-high status is associated with dramatically stronger WRN dependency, now independently validated globally and robust to TMB, screen quality, library, growth, lineage, and matched-omics context; (2) SMARCA4 loss is associated with dramatically stronger SMARCA2 dependency, validated globally in ARID1A-intact and ARID1A-loss settings (H28/R40, H49/R39) and robust to screen quality and KY library; and (3) KEAP1 loss is associated with dramatically weaker NFE2L2 dependency, validated in STK11-intact lines and robust in STK11-loss, high-screen-quality, KY-library, and matched-omics settings. These are strong internal associations in the supplied lung cell-line dataset, not evidence of causal gene action or generalizable biology.

Negative findings remain useful. EGFR amplification is not supported for stronger EGFR dependency after validation (H3/R3+R13). BRAF V600E is not supported for stronger BRAF dependency (H2/R2). KRAS mutation is not supported for stronger RIT1 dependency (H9/R9), and BRAF V600E among KRAS-wildtype lines is not supported for stronger RIT1 dependency (H79/R51). PIK3CA mutation is not supported for stronger STAT3 dependency (H57/R33). NF1 loss among KRAS-wildtype lines is not supported for stronger RIT1 dependency (H60/R35). MYC amplification is rejected for stronger RPL11 dependency globally (H12/R12) and unresolved but not supported among high-MYC-expression lines (H82/R52). Research marker controls do not reproduce the magnitude of the accepted effects.

Unresolved uncertainty is concentrated in smaller or co-altered contexts: the EGFR reversal claims remain unresolved (H62 active, H85 active), ERBB2 amplification remains near-null or unresolved (H4/H75), KRAS-mutation KRAS dependency remains weakly positive but unresolved (H1/H15/H59), MDM2/TP53 dependency remains unresolved (H5/H78), MYC-related dependencies under high transcriptomic MYC are mostly untested or unresolved (H80-H84), and broad controls such as research-marker associations and library/low-serum robustness remain active. The two interaction tests, H64 and H66, are closed as unresolved because their intervals include null and do not establish meaningful effect modification.

The most informative next analysis should be independent validation of the original global SMARCA4-loss/SMARCA2 claim H7 if validation requests remain useful, because it is the only one of the three core global accepted associations not yet directly validated. In parallel, the highest-value discovery follow-ups are the remaining active high-MYC-expression claims and research-marker/library controls; the EGFR reversal claims can remain secondary unless a larger or co-amplification-isolated subgroup gives an interval that clears the EGFR threshold with an independent replication.

This round adds orthogonal technical, genomic, transcriptional, and pathway-isolation tests for the strongest accepted dataset associations, then adds a few high-value untested associations for outcomes that remain mostly null. The first three proposals filter to lines with Cas9 activity of at least 80%. If the accepted WRN/MSI-high, SMARCA2/SMARCA4-loss, and NFE2L2/KEAP1-loss effects persist under high Cas9 activity, that argues against the possibility that they are artifacts of weak or variable Cas9 cutting efficiency. A null or marked attenuation would suggest that Cas9 QC context matters and would change the strength of the dataset-level inference, though it still would not establish causality. The fourth proposal tests WRN/MSI-high within lower mutation-burden lines, complementing the accepted high-mutation-burden restriction. This asks whether the WRN association is specific to MSI biology rather than being merely a surrogate for high tumor mutation burden. The high-Cas9 filters for SMARCA2 and NFE2L2, the high mutation-burden filter for SMARCA2, and the fast-proliferation filter for NFE2L2 complete a set of context robustness tests for the core triad. If these large effects remain far above the approximate 10%-of-absolute-score thresholds, confidence increases that they are stable dataset-specific associations rather than context-specific anomalies. The EGFR and ERBB2 proposals refine the earlier near-null RTK amplification analyses by isolating likely single-RTK/driver contexts: EGFR-amplified lines that are ERBB2-amplification-negative and KRAS-mutation-negative, and ERBB2-amplified lines that are EGFR-amplification-negative and KRAS-mutation-negative. The stronger-dependency direction is registered because KRAS co-mutation can mask RTK dependency and because the EGFR ERBB2-negative signal had a weakly positive discovery estimate in the opposite direction to the rejected weaker-dependency hypothesis. Plausible alternatives are null, attenuation due to reduced cell numbers, or a genuinely absent RTK-amplification dependency signal in this dataset. The TMED10 proposal extends the transcriptionally active MYC strategy already registered for DHX9, POLR2A, USP7, KIF18A, and STAT3. If MYC amplification matters only when MYC is highly expressed, TMED10 should show a stronger association in that subset. The STAT3/PTEN-loss, KIF18A/RB1-loss, and KRAS/STK11-loss proposals are scientifically exploratory pathway hypotheses: PI3K pathway loss-of-function may alter STAT3 dependency, cell-cycle/RB pathway loss may alter mitotic KIF18A dependency, and STK11 loss may alter KRAS dependency through metabolic or signaling context. The expected direction for each is stronger dependency, i.e. a more negative score in the exposed group, but these are falsifiable and near-null or opposite directions would be informative. All conclusions will remain associations in this supplied lung cell-line dataset; they will not by themselves prove causal gene dependency or generalizable biology.

I selected the twelve newly registered discovery hypotheses because they provide new samples and orthogonal stress tests for the strongest dataset-specific associations. H86-H88 test whether the accepted WRN/MSI-high, SMARCA2/SMARCA4-loss, and NFE2L2/KEAP1-loss effects persist when restricted to lines with relatively high measured Cas9 activity (>=80%), which assesses whether these very large associations could be artifacts of poor or variable Cas9 cutting efficiency. H89 complements the accepted high-mutation-burden WRN/MSI-high test by checking the effect in lower mutation-burden lines, helping distinguish a specific MSI/high-WRN association from a generic high-TMB association. H96 and H97 further test the accepted SMARCA2 and NFE2L2 associations in biologically relevant subsets: relatively high mutation burden for SMARCA4 loss and faster proliferation for KEAP1 loss. H90 and H91 refine RTK amplification interpretation by requiring absence of KRAS mutation as well as absence of the reciprocal amplification, making EGFR-amplified and ERBB2-amplified groups more likely to represent relatively driver-isolated contexts. H92 tests whether MYC amplification is associated with transcriptionally active MYC-dependent TMED10 dependency, extending the high-MYC-expression strategy already used for other MYC-related dependencies. H93-H95 add exploratory pathway-specific tests for otherwise unresolved outcomes: PTEN loss with STAT3 dependency, RB1 loss with KIF18A dependency, and STK11 loss with KRAS dependency. These analyses were chosen instead of rerunning already tested claims because they add new information about technical robustness, genomic context, co-alteration isolation, and pathway hypotheses without consuming slots on comparisons whose data are already known.

The new results mainly confirm that the three very large core associations are not sensitive to technical Cas9-activity restriction or biologically motivated subsetting. Approximate 10% clinical thresholds from population absolute mean scores are about +0.030 for WRN, +0.042 for SMARCA2, +0.009 for NFE2L2, +0.028 for STAT3, +0.026 for ERBB2, +0.024 for KRAS, +0.025 for TMED10, and +0.026 for KIF18A. H86/R54 gives WRN/MSI-high a signed effect +0.776 with lower bound +0.728 under high Cas9 activity; H87/R55 gives SMARCA2/SMARCA4-loss +0.788 with lower bound +0.756; H88/R56 gives KEAP1-loss weaker NFE2L2 +0.800 with lower bound +0.769. These are all far above their thresholds and far from null, supporting acceptance and closure. H89/R57 tests WRN/MSI-high among lower mutation-burden lines; despite only 21 exposed lines, the estimate is +0.798 and the lower bound is +0.706. This is valid and strongly supports that MSI-high is not merely acting as a generic high-TMB surrogate in this dataset. H96/R64 and H97/R65 similarly accept SMARCA2/SMARCA4-loss under high mutation burden and KEAP1-loss under faster proliferation. The RTK and transcriptional-MYC isolation tests do not support the registered positive directions as clinically meaningful. H90/R58 has a positive point estimate +0.018 but interval -0.012 to +0.048; because the upper bound crosses the EGFR threshold, it remains unresolved. H91/R59 has upper bound +0.023, below the ERBB2 threshold of about +0.026, so clinically meaningful stronger ERBB2 dependency in the isolated EGFR-negative KRAS-WT context is rejected. H92/R60 is near-null for MYC-related TMED10, interval -0.030 to +0.031, unresolved. H94/R62 has upper bound +0.036 above the KIF18A threshold, but includes null, so RB1-loss stronger KIF18A remains unresolved. H95/R63 has upper bound +0.018 below the KRAS threshold, so STK11-loss stronger KRAS is rejected. The major new finding is H93/R61: PTEN loss is associated with much stronger STAT3 dependency, signed estimate +0.267, interval +0.215 to +0.319, with cells 266 versus 1734. This effect is roughly 9 to 11 times the approximate STAT3 clinical threshold and very precisely estimated, so I accept it in this dataset but keep it active because it is a newly discovered association with multiplicity and confounding concerns. I request independent validation of H93 rather than H7 because H7's global SMARCA2 effect is already supported by multiple accepted and validated context refinements, whereas H93 is a new large claim whose internal validity would be most directly strengthened by independent replication. These remain dataset-specific associations, not causal or generalizable claims.

The independent validation answers the response deadlines for the ARID1A-restricted SMARCA2 claims and confirms the new PTEN-loss STAT3 claim. For H49, SMARCA4 loss among ARID1A-loss lines is associated with far stronger SMARCA2 dependency. Independent validation R39 gives signed estimate +0.8105 with interval +0.7431 to +0.8779 in cells 95 versus 358, closely matching discovery R29 estimate +0.8143. The approximate 10% clinical threshold for SMARCA2, using the population absolute mean score about 0.415, is about +0.0415; the validation lower bound is roughly 18 times that threshold. H49 remains accepted and closed. For H28, SMARCA4 loss among ARID1A-intact lines is associated with far stronger SMARCA2 dependency, independent validation R40 +0.8118, interval +0.7784 to +0.8452, cells 321 versus 1250, again far above the SMARCA2 threshold and consistent with discovery R14. H28 remains accepted and closed. Together with H7, H30, H31, H52, H71, H72, H77-equivalent robustness claims, H87, H96, and the ARID1A-intact/loss validations, this makes the SMARCA4-loss/SMARCA2 association one of the most internally supported dataset findings. It remains an association in this supplied dataset, not a causal or generalizable biological claim. For H93, PTEN loss is associated with substantially stronger STAT3 dependency globally. Independent validation R66 gives signed estimate +0.2919 with interval +0.2135 to +0.3704 in cells 265 versus 1735, very close to discovery R61 estimate +0.2674. The approximate STAT3 clinical threshold is about +0.028, so the validation point estimate is roughly ten times the threshold and its lower bound is roughly seven times the threshold. Even under the stringent independent validation interval, this is scientifically meaningful in this dataset. I accept H93 and close the original global claim. Its smaller magnitude than WRN/MSI-high, SMARCA2/SMARCA4-loss, and NFE2L2/KEAP1-loss does not make it marginal by the stated threshold; it is precisely estimated and replicated. Context and specificity tests remain valuable and are represented by separate active claims. I registered additional PTEN context tests and PTEN specificity tests: whether the PTEN/STAT3 effect persists or changes in PIK3CA-mutant and TP53-loss settings, and whether PTEN loss also produces large associations with SMARCA2 among SMARCA4-intact lines or WRN among MSI-low lines. If PTEN loss is large across unrelated main-driver strata, the STAT3 association may be less specific or confounded by co-alteration patterns; if it remains near-null there, the PTEN/STAT3 signal becomes more distinctive. Other active priorities remain high-MYC-expression dependency claims, EGFR reversal only if new interval evidence appears, and remaining controls or robustness gaps.

I propose effect-modification and specificity tests that follow from the strongest dataset-specific findings rather than repeating mean-difference presence tests that have already been shown or rejected. First, PTEN-loss/STAT3 is now accepted and independently validated, but its internal interpretation still needs to be distinguished from a general co-alteration effect or a broader PI3K-TP53-RAS network effect. Interactions of PTEN loss with PIK3CA mutation, TP53 loss, and KRAS mutation test whether the PTEN effect is amplified, attenuated, or essentially constant across these common co-drivers. The additional PTEN analysis restricted to TP53-intact and PIK3CA-intact lines asks whether the global PTEN/STAT3 association survives when two likely co-mutant contexts are removed. A clinically meaningful attenuated effect in these strata would suggest that the global estimate is context-dependent or confounded by co-alteration patterns, whereas persistence would strengthen the association in this dataset. Second, I add an interaction for the unresolved MDM2/TP53-loss comparison with CDKN2A loss. The global MDM2 estimate is small, but effect modification could be clinically relevant even when the mean difference is not, and the TP53-CDKN2A p53-axis context is scientifically motivated. Third, the core WRN/MSI-high, SMARCA2/SMARCA4-loss, and NFE2L2/KEAP1-loss associations are already robust in mean-difference tests within KY library and adenocarcinoma subsets. The new interaction tests ask whether the size of those associations changes by library or subtype. A near-null interaction would argue that the large effects are broadly shared across these technical and histologic contexts; a large positive or negative interaction would identify important subgroup-specific attenuation or amplification. Fourth, PTEN loss is tested against KRAS dependency as a broad specificity probe. PTEN loss could plausibly alter KRAS or STAT3 through PI3K/RAS feedback pathways, so a large PTEN/KRAS association would reduce the outcome specificity of PTEN/STAT3. A near-null PTEN/KRAS result, together with specificity tests already registered for SMARCA2 and WRN, would make PTEN/STAT3 appear more selective in this dataset. All proposals remain comparisons of measured associations within the supplied lung cell-line dataset and should not be interpreted as causal gene dependency or generalizable biology until independently replicated or externally contextualized.

I selected the twelve newly registered claims H109 through H120 because they are the only analyses that provide new information relative to the current ledger and they directly follow from the strongest accepted associations. H109-H112 test whether the newly accepted and validated PTEN-loss/STAT3 association is modified by PIK3CA mutation, TP53 loss, or KRAS mutation, or persists when PIK3CA- and TP53-co-mutated contexts are removed. This distinguishes a relatively stable PTEN/STAT3 association from one largely driven by common co-alteration patterns. H113 asks whether the otherwise small global TP53-loss association with MDM2 dependency has a clinically meaningful interaction with CDKN2A loss in the p53 axis. H114-H119 test effect modification for the three very large core associations by library and adenocarcinoma subtype. Because mean differences within KY and adenocarcinoma subsets are already large and accepted, these interactions ask whether the effect sizes differ across technical and histologic contexts; near-null interactions would support broad consistency, whereas large interactions would identify important attenuation or amplification. H120 is a specificity probe: if PTEN loss is also strongly associated with KRAS dependency, the PTEN/STAT3 finding is less specific; if near-null, PTEN/STAT3 appears more selective among tested outcomes. I did not select previously tested claims because cached comparisons reuse known data and would not add evidence. All conclusions will remain associations in the supplied lung cell-line dataset and will not be interpreted as causal dependencies or generalizable biology.

I audited the twelve interaction and specificity tests for clinically meaningful effect modification and outcome specificity using approximate 10% outcome-specific thresholds: about +0.028 for STAT3, +0.030 for WRN, +0.042 for SMARCA2, +0.027 for MDM2, and +0.024 for KRAS. The clean-context PTEN-loss result is the key new acceptance: in lines that are both PIK3CA-intact and TP53-intact, PTEN loss is associated with substantially stronger STAT3 dependency, R70 +0.293 with lower bound +0.228. This is roughly eight times the STAT3 threshold and is not compatible with the interpretation that the global PTEN/STAT3 association is confined to PIK3CA- or TP53-co-altered contexts. I accept H112 in this dataset and request independent validation because it is a newly accepted refined subset of an already validated global association and could strengthen the context-specific claim. The interaction tests for PTEN/STAT3 with PIK3CA or KRAS are underpowered and broad, R67 and R69 include null and clinically meaningful effects in both directions, so they remain unresolved; H109 stays active because PIK3CA context is biologically salient, while H111 is deferred. The TP53-loss PTEN/STAT3 interaction rejects the registered positive direction, R68 upper bound +0.024 below the STAT3 threshold, although the negative signed interval suggests possible attenuation rather than amplification; I closed H110 and registered a new opposite-direction attenuation claim to test that possibility separately. The MDM2 TP53-loss interaction with CDKN2A loss is near-null but still unresolved, R71 interval extends beyond the MDM2 threshold, so H113 remains active as a secondary p53-axis follow-up. The core associations were also tested for library and histologic effect modification. WRN/MSI-high in KY rejects the registered positive interaction, R72 upper bound -0.010 below the WRN threshold, and suggests attenuation rather than amplification; H114 is closed and a new attenuation claim is registered, but the opposite-direction effect is not yet clinically robust because its lower bound would be only about +0.010. WRN/adenocarcinoma interaction remains unresolved but deferred, R73 upper bound crosses the WRN threshold. SMARCA2/SMARCA4-loss interaction in KY is near the SMARCA2 threshold but imprecise, R74 lower bound just below null; H116 remains active. SMARCA2/adenocarcinoma interaction rejects the registered positive direction, R75 upper bound +0.020 below threshold. NFE2L2/KEAP1-loss interactions with KY and adenocarcinoma are near null but intervals remain wider than the small NFE2L2 threshold, so H118 and H119 remain unresolved but deferred. The PTEN-loss stronger-KRAS specificity probe rejects the registered direction, R78 upper bound +0.008 below the KRAS threshold; this supports outcome selectivity for PTEN/STAT3 over PTEN/KRAS in this dataset. Overall, the new evidence strengthens PTEN/STAT3 context robustness and the specificity of PTEN/STAT3 relative to KRAS dependency, but most interaction conclusions remain imprecise and should not be overinterpreted.

Independent validation resolves the outstanding deadline for WRN/MSI-high and confirms the context-restricted PTEN-loss claim, while rejecting the high-MYC RPL11 follow-up. For H6, MSI-high is associated with dramatically stronger WRN dependency. Discovery R6 was +0.790 (interval +0.760 to +0.819), and independent validation R53 gives +0.790 with independent interval +0.736 to +0.843, cells 117 versus 1883. Using the approximate 10% outcome-specific threshold for WRN of about +0.030, the validation lower bound is roughly 25 times the threshold. This is one of the strongest and most internally replicated dataset associations. For H112, PTEN loss is associated with substantially stronger STAT3 dependency among PIK3CA-intact and TP53-intact lines. Discovery R70 was +0.293 with lower bound +0.228, and validation R79 gives +0.236 with independent interval +0.140 to +0.332, cells 160 versus 1153. Against the approximate STAT3 threshold of about +0.028, the validation lower bound is about five times the threshold. This rejects the concern that the global PTEN/STAT3 signal is confined to PIK3CA- or TP53-co-altered contexts, although it remains an association rather than a causal claim. For H37, MYC-amplified lines with high MYC expression were tested for stronger RPL11 dependency. Discovery R38 was imprecise and near null, and independent validation R80 gives a signed estimate of -0.035, interval -0.080 to +0.009. The positive-direction upper bound is below the approximate RPL11 threshold of about +0.025 and the point estimate is in the opposite direction. I therefore reject this registered clinically meaningful positive effect and close the investigation. Overall, the supported dataset-specific findings are: MSI-high is associated with far stronger WRN dependency; SMARCA4 loss is associated with far stronger SMARCA2 dependency, including in ARID1A-intact and ARID1A-loss contexts; KEAP1 loss is associated with far weaker NFE2L2 dependency; and PTEN loss is associated with substantially stronger STAT3 dependency, globally and in a PIK3CA- and TP53-intact subset. Negative findings include rejection of several registered directions, such as PTEN-loss stronger KRAS dependency, amplification by KY library for WRN/MSI-high, amplification by adenocarcinoma subtype for SMARCA2/SMARCA4-loss, TP53-loss amplification of PTEN/STAT3, and the high-MYC RPL11 effect. Unresolved issues remain around possible attenuation of PTEN/STAT3 in TP53-loss lines, attenuation of WRN/MSI-high in KY-library screens, and many underpowered effect-modification tests. The next most informative analyses are outcome specificity probes for the accepted predictors and outcomes: whether MSI-high, SMARCA4 loss, KEAP1 loss, and PTEN loss selectively associate with their focal dependencies rather than broadly altering multiple dependency scores. This can sharpen whether these are marker-specific associations in the supplied lung cell-line dataset rather than general co-alteration patterns.
